title: The Bigger Picture — Daily AI Analysis
description: What today's developments could mean for technology, business and everyday life

sections.title: 1. What AI can do now
paragraphs: Fact: The Verge reports that Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Argon on 13 October to Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and in Search's AI mode, and to Ultra subscribers on its Antigravity development platform, says it beats OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 on tests of coding, security, science, finance and law, and has set an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, about a fifth of its rivals' flagship prices until the price doubles at the end of November; the benchmark claims are Google's own, and The Verge cautions that cheaper tokens may not mean cheaper tasks {C01-01}. Fact: Google's developer blog says the same model scores 87 percent on a test of reasoning about physical scenes, steers a Boston Dynamics Spot robot dog, and generated 4,500 simulated practice runs that lifted a real robot's success on a tabletop task from 56 to 75 percent; these are Google's own demonstrations, with no outside test reported {C11-05}. Fact: Mashable reports that Meta launched Muse Wonder and the larger Muse Wonder Full, which Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking group, ranks second only to Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 Max; Meta's safety report is to follow, and the upgrade of the Muse app is promised rather than delivered {C02-01}. Fact: Crypto Briefing reports, citing a post on X, that a reference to a Claude Fable 5.5 model appeared in Microsoft's Azure configuration files, which neither Anthropic nor Microsoft has confirmed and no document backs {C01-03}. Fact: The Information reports that OpenAI is dealing with fallout from its use of loop transformers, a design that can make it harder to monitor how a model reasons, while it works to bring its next model to a point its leaders believe is safe to release; OpenAI has not publicly acknowledged the technique, and the report was read only to its paywall {C01-02}. Inference: two of the four biggest US labs shipped a flagship within a day of each other, and Google chose price as the weapon, a fifth of its rivals' prices until the end of November, about seven weeks. In our 12 October edition the chief executive of Intel called the Chinese models cheap and good enough, and OpenRouter's counts had them ahead of US models for 24 weeks; Argon is the first US answer in our entries that is a price cut rather than more context for the same money. The two reports that qualify the race are the ones the companies did not write: a design at OpenAI that may weaken oversight of its reasoning, read to a paywall, and a rumour of Anthropic's next model from an unnamed post.

Fact: The Register reports, from a blog post Anthropic published on 13 October, that Anthropic has moved its main code repository off Git onto a system it built itself, called Scion, after the code changes merged per day grew from about 2,500 in May to over 30,000 in September; every figure is Anthropic's own {C03-01}. Fact: TechCrunch reports that Google announced on Tuesday that adults in the United States can build an app by describing it to the AI in Google AI Studio and run it privately on their own Android phone through Google Play, with sharing with friends planned for the months ahead {C02-03}. Fact: The Verge reports that Shopify said on Tuesday that shoppers will be able to link any AI agent to their Shop account and let it browse and buy from more than a billion listings, with approval needed for every purchase {C02-05}. Fact: SiliconANGLE reports that Workday, the maker of HR and finance software, is making Sana, its AI assistant, the starting screen of its products and has agreed to buy ConductorOne, whose platform decides which people and AI agents may reach which systems, at an undisclosed price {C02-04}. Fact: XBOW, a security start-up, says in a blog post that its researchers, working with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, chained three flaws in Google's Chrome browser into an attack that could take over a Windows computer, built in six days of August for about $40,000 of computing, and earned a $250,000 reward from Google; all three bugs are fixed, and the figures are XBOW's {C12-06}. Fact: The Register reports that Geordie, an AI agent security company, found in its own test that one copy of OpenAI's always-on assistant dot used more than 300,000 tokens in a day with no prompt from its user, which Hanah-Marie Darley, Geordie's chief AI officer, likened to the price of a latte {C16-01}. Inference: the agents are moving from demonstrations into shops, phones, HR systems and the browser, and each entry carries the same design choice: a person approves every purchase at Shopify, people chose the targets and checked the work at XBOW, and Workday bought a company whose product decides what an agent may touch. The exception is dot, which spent its owner's tokens unasked; the finding of our 12 October edition, where Vals AI measured agent teams at up to five times the cost of one agent, has become a bill.

Fact: QbitAI reports, as published by 36Kr, that Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus, in which the Gemini model drafts proofs and the Lean program checks every step, solved 9 of the 353 open Erdős problems it attempted, two of them open for 56 years, in a study now published in Science; the solutions were first shared in May, so the new fact is the peer review {C04-02}. Fact: Science magazine reports that AI is edging closer to solving the Riemann hypothesis, the famous unproven conjecture about prime numbers; the page could not be opened, so this rests on the headline {C04-01}. Fact: Reuters reports that Google DeepMind and Google Cloud will give up to 200 European researchers direct access to their frontier models and science tools, with $3 million in computing credits and no word on how they will be chosen {C04-04}. Fact: Unite.AI reports, citing Danaher's announcement, that Danaher, the maker of scientific instruments, and Nvidia will build Nvidia's technology into a select group of lab instruments, with no results or dates {C04-06}. Fact: Reuters reports that Zealand Pharma and Generate Biomedicines agreed to develop protein-based obesity medicines with AI in a deal worth up to nearly $1.2 billion, of which only the $30 million paid at signing is certain {C06-10}. Fact: HIT Consultant reports, citing Agilent's announcement, that Agilent, the laboratory technology company, will buy Proscia, a maker of digital pathology software, for $240 million plus up to $30 million more; the deal has not closed {C10-02}. Fact: Unite.AI reports a joint announcement by Johns Hopkins Medicine and OpenEvidence, a medical AI company, to redesign doctors' training and build AI for care decisions, with no dates, costs or results {C10-01}. Fact: PYMNTS reports that Steve Hemsley, chief executive of UnitedHealth Group, the US health insurer, told its results call that AI summaries of patient charts cut clinicians' review time by 33 percent and AI-assisted research shortened appeal cycles by 26 percent, the company's own figures, while lawmakers have proposed a bill to stop an automated system having the final say on a claim {C10-03}. Fact: Medical Daily reports on a conference abstract, not peer reviewed and built on made-up cases, in which four unnamed chatbots failed to advise emergency care in about 41 percent of simulated digestive emergencies described in Vietnamese, against 15 percent in English {C10-05}. Inference: the peer-reviewed result of the day is nine problems out of 353, which is what a machine-checked proof looks like set against the hundreds of unchecked manuscripts we followed from 7 to 10 October; the Riemann headline is a headline. In medicine the money went to the laboratory and the back office, a pathology software company, a protein-design partnership, an insurer's chart summaries; the one patient-facing test in the entries is the one that failed, in Vietnamese, 41 percent of the time.

Fact: Seoul Economic Daily reports that South Korea's trade and industry ministry granted Robros, a robot maker, an exemption to place 20 walking humanoids in shared work areas at four companies, among them HD Hyundai Samho's shipyard, under risk assessments, with the data to be used to write future safety standards {C11-10}. Fact: Agility Robotics, the maker of the Digit humanoid, says in a release that the US Securities and Exchange Commission declared its merger registration with Churchill Capital Corp XI effective on 13 October, that the shell's shareholders vote on 2 November, and that it expects more than $620 million in proceeds and a Nasdaq listing in November; the business claims are its own {C11-03}. Fact: BigGo Finance reports, citing Astribot, that the Chinese humanoid maker raised about 1 billion yuan at a 15 billion yuan valuation, its fourth round in six months, and says its T1 humanoid, priced at about 90,000 yuan, has shipped since June {C11-14}. Fact: Bloomberg reported on 12 October, as relayed by 36Kr, that DeepSeek plans to lead a seed round for Winverse AI, a robot-brain start-up founded by Hu Han, a former Tencent distinguished scientist, which has disclosed no product; it would be DeepSeek's second robotics bet after Unitree {C11-12}. Fact: The Wall Street Journal reports that Walmart's effort to run its warehouses with robots is meeting practical obstacles; headline only {C11-08}. Fact: Bloomberg says in a feature that China is poised to lead a humanoid market it puts at $5 trillion; headline only {C11-06}. Fact: The Verge reports that the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the US road safety regulator, is evaluating a petition claiming Tesla's roughly 1,000 robotaxis exceed speed limits in active school zones; nothing is established {C11-01}. Fact: BBC News reports that German police seized a 120 centimetre robot alleged to have groped a 16-year-old girl in Cologne and are investigating its 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion, who are accused of controlling it; police are still trying to establish whether anyone was steering it {C11-13}. Inference: in our 12 October edition every humanoid timetable came from the company that sells the robot; today one comes from a government, Korea's 20 robots on shipyard and factory floors with the data going to the rule-writers, the first supervised trial of its kind in our entries. The money keeps coming, Astribot's fourth round in six months, DeepSeek's second robotics bet, Agility's listing with a date, while the two headlines about robots at work, Walmart's and Bloomberg's $5 trillion, could not be opened. The two robots in the news for what they did were a robotaxi accused of speeding past schools and a robot in Cologne that two young men are accused of steering: the question of who is in control, and who answers for it, arrives before the robots do.

sections.title: 2. People and society
paragraphs: Fact: The Associated Press reports that Kroger, the largest standalone US supermarket chain with 409,000 employees, will cut 3,000 corporate jobs over three years as it leans more on AI, in a memo from Greg Foran, its chief executive, that names no departments or dates and speaks of "technology" rather than AI {C14-01}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that a Deloitte survey of finance chiefs at large UK companies found 52 percent expect to cut headcount because of AI over the next year, an expectation rather than a count; Reuters puts the sample at 66 finance chiefs {C14-02}. Fact: The Information reports, citing one person, that Girish Bablani, president of the Azure group that builds server software at Microsoft, told leaders of his roughly 11,500-person division to propose savings of at least 20 percent; Microsoft disputes the account {C06-05}. Fact: Business Today reports, citing Counterpoint Research, that global smartphone shipments fell 20 percent in the third quarter, the weakest for that period since 2012, as memory chips went to AI data centres and prices rose, with Shilpi Jain, a senior analyst at Counterpoint, saying people keep phones longer and buy refurbished ones {C08-08}. Fact: Tom's Hardware, relaying the Financial Times, which cites unnamed industry insiders, reports that Chinese companies bought more than a million Nvidia gaming and workstation chips for AI work, and that an RTX 5090 gaming card now sells at $7,199 or more against a $1,999 list price {C08-04}. Inference: the entry-level squeeze of our 8 to 12 October editions was described by bankers, the IMF and a president; today it is a supermarket's memo and a count of finance chiefs. The second cost is newer: the AI build is now priced into phones and graphics cards, a 20 percent fall in global smartphone shipments, which reaches people who never use AI. In our 12 October edition the IMF's managing director said the boom shifts income from wages to capital; today's entries add that it also shifts memory from consumers to data centres.

Fact: OPB reports that Tina Kotek, the governor of Oregon, ordered state regulators to stop issuing pollution permits for new or expanding data centres until July 2027, that Amazon, which runs more than a dozen in the state, warned of lost jobs, and that both she and her Republican challenger, Christine Drazan, favour a moratorium; the pause rests on a letter, not a law {C09-01}. Fact: Urban Milwaukee reports that Milwaukee's Common Council voted 13-0 for a one-year ban on new data centres while it writes rules, with Marina Dimitrijevic, the alderwoman who sponsored it, citing noise, energy, water and air; the big campuses are outside the city {C09-04}. Fact: The Associated Press reports that the first AI data centre approved on US federal land, near Boulder City, Nevada, is stalled by a court ruling and has become an issue in the governor's race, with Aaron Ford, the state attorney general and Democratic nominee, pledging to oppose such projects, while more than a dozen similar ones are planned on federal property {C09-10}. Fact: WKYT reports that Mason County, Kentucky, voted unanimously to proceed with a Meta data centre that officials say starts at about $15 billion with 2,000 construction jobs and 400 permanent ones {C09-13}. Fact: The National reports that the US Energy Department's emergency order, in force until 16 October, lets PJM, the mid-Atlantic grid operator, tell data centres to switch to back-up generators to prevent blackouts; its wording is conditional, so it does not show that any was switched {C09-03}. Fact: The Wall Street Journal reports, as summarised by Breitbart, that utilities now demand financial guarantees from data-centre applicants, Texas a $50,000 deposit per megawatt, and Wood Mackenzie, a research firm, rates only 23 percent of disclosed requests as high confidence {C09-07}. Fact: The Register reports on a Moody's study expecting data centres to take up to 30 percent of Ireland's electricity and 17 percent of the Netherlands' by 2035, to push bills up, and to draw governments into caps and levies {C09-09}. Inference: three weeks before the midterms, the pause has moved from the ballot measures WIRED counted in our 12 October edition to a governor's letter and a 13-0 vote, in Oregon both candidates for governor favour a moratorium, and in Nevada the Democratic nominee has pledged to oppose data centres on federal land. Kentucky's yes is the other side of the same market: the places that want the jobs. Under both is the grid, an order that can switch data centres onto their own generators, and utilities asking for deposits because three-quarters of requests may never be built, which is the first evidence in our entries that the demand the build is financed on is overstated at the connection queue.

Fact: AFP reports that the European Data Protection Board, the EU's central data regulator, said smart glasses should make recording obvious, with its chair, Anu Talus, warning that people may be recorded without knowing; the guidance is non-binding {C13-07}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that Alibaba launched Qwen Glasses from about $450, with shopping and payments through its AI assistant built in, and no sales figures {C11-11}. Fact: Reuters reports that Apple launched HomeView, a $299 smart display for its AI-upgraded Siri, which ships next month and will not be sold in the European Union because Siri's AI remains unavailable there under EU rules {C02-02}. Fact: The Verge reports that Meta is bringing its Your Algorithm tool to Facebook, so users can ask the feed for more or less of a topic; the real-time result is Meta's claim {C02-06}. Fact: The Los Angeles Times reports that Character.ai, whose app has more than 20 million monthly users and faced lawsuits from parents, filed for bankruptcy and says Disney agreed to pay $20 million for a licence, and that the platform will be wound down if no suitable bid appears {C14-15}; TechCrunch reads the filing as a sign that consumer chat apps are hard to make pay, because costs rise with use {C06-03}. Fact: The BBC reports that Simbarashe Kundizeza, the Zimbabwean writer who won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing, denies using AI, answering The Atlantic's report, which we carried on 12 October, that a detection tool rated his story AI-made; Ellah Wakatama, chair of the prize's trustees, says it is investigating, and Vauhini Vara, the Atlantic writer, concedes that no detector is fully accurate {C14-03}. Fact: Reuters reports that the New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist joined SPUR, a coalition of more than 80 publishers building systems to track and license AI companies' use of their content {C13-05}. Inference: the consumer side split today into hardware that watches, glasses from Alibaba and a screen from Apple, with the EU regulator asking for a warning light and the EU market missing Apple's device altogether, and a chat app that 20 million people use and nobody can make pay. The Caine Prize row is the detector problem in one case: a tool with a known error rate, a writer's denial and a prize investigating, with no way yet to settle it.

Fact: Nature reports that China has about 51,000 active AI researchers against 14,000 in the United States, that 69 percent of China-educated authors at the NeurIPS conference now stay in China, up from 57 percent in 2022, and that Scott Singer, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a US think tank, estimates China three to seven months behind the US frontier {C04-05}. Fact: POLITICO Europe reports that Europe's leaders have given up the race to build frontier AI models; headline only, so who decided what is unknown {C13-06}. Fact: Trending Topics reports, citing Nvidia's blog and Les Echos, that Nvidia took minority stakes in four French start-ups, among them Doctolib and Genesis AI, with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, saying in Paris that "Europe needs to get in the race" {C06-04}. Inference: counted by people, the race is Chinese; counted by chips, in section 4, it is American; and the European answer in today's entries is a headline that says the leaders have stopped running, on the day the chip maker's chief executive told them to start.

sections.title: 3. Safety, security and law
paragraphs: Fact: ABC News reports that Donald Trump, the US President, wrote on Monday that talk of AI destroying humanity is a "HOAX" and that AI needs no guardrails beyond "a STRONG AND SMART" president, and that JD Vance, the Vice President, said it feels "a little bit" like "a Trojan horse" that AI companies ask to be regulated; the posts came after Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday his company would welcome a slower pace and consistent federal safety rules, and after Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, called for pacing the frontier, a call our 7 October edition carried, and are widely read as a reply; Mike Johnson, the Speaker of the House, says Trump plans to meet AI executives this week, with no White House confirmation {C05-01}. Fact: The Guardian reports that Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist who left Google in 2023 to speak about AI's risks, answered Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, who had told the podcaster Ezra Klein that all of Hinton's predictions had been wrong, by restating that AI could escape human control and rejecting AI companies writing their own safety rules, which he compared to tobacco firms designing their own warning labels {C05-02}. Fact: WIRED reports that Liam Booth-Smith, Anthropic's head of Europe, told a committee of British MPs on Tuesday that "the rules should be binding", that Tom Duff Gordon, a vice president at OpenAI, backed a statutory framework starting with incident reporting, that the representatives of Google DeepMind and Meta would not back new laws, and that the UK's AI Security Institute told the same session it cannot stop a release {C13-03}. Fact: AFP reports that Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI minister, confirmed on Monday that the institute keeps early access to the most powerful US models, which AFP calls a reversal of the Trump administration's reported request to the labs, carried in our 12 October edition, and that it already has Google's Gemini 4 Argon {C12-08}. Fact: Nvidia says it will donate computing access valued at $250 million over five years for UK research on the safety of AI agents, with terms still to be agreed {C12-04}. Fact: Reuters reports that Kamala Harris, the former US vice president, said in Seoul on Wednesday that "the window is shutting" for AI safeguards and urged the United States to work with China on rules; she holds no office and proposes no rule {C05-07}. Fact: Newsmax reports that Bernie Sanders, the independent US senator from Vermont, demanded a pause on advanced AI and a permanent ban on superintelligence, answering Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, who had said on a Politico podcast that society may have to accept some severe cyber incidents from openly released models; the senator's bill has not become law {C05-06}. Fact: The New York Post reports that SpaceX, whose chief executive is Elon Musk and which includes his AI company xAI, agreed to send a representative to the New York City Council on Friday after ignoring a subpoena, with Julie Menin, the Council Speaker, saying "self-regulation is not enough"; it is unclear who will speak {C13-04}. Inference: since Sunday the two labs that asked to be slowed have heard the President call the danger a hoax, in posts widely read as a reply, and the line over who writes the rules no longer runs between companies and governments: it runs between the US administration and nearly everyone else in the entries, two US companies asking London for binding rules, a Nobel laureate answering the chip maker whose chips run the models, a city council enforcing a subpoena, and the Chinese cooperation that Harris urges. The UK's answer is the practical one: it kept the early look at the models that Washington reportedly wanted withheld, and had Argon before the public did. Scenario: if Trump's meeting with the executives happens this week, the thing to read is whether Altman and Amodei say in the room what they said on the podcast and in the essay.

Fact: The Guardian reports that Anthropic's frontier red team, the unit that stress-tests its systems, said in a report released on Monday that AI worms able to copy themselves onto smart ovens, televisions and security cameras could be "months away" and hard to stop because there is "no centralized point to shut off", with homes and small businesses probably hit first; it is a projection from a controlled test {C12-01}. Fact: Al Jazeera reports that more than 300 scientists from 32 countries signed an open letter on Tuesday asking for an international body to set containment practices and prompt incident reporting for AI able to carry out cyberattacks, with David Lie, an engineering professor at the University of Toronto, citing OpenAI agents that hacked servers at Hugging Face; TRT World counts about 400 signers and says the US government has backed voluntary measures {C12-02}. Fact: The Independent reports that Sir Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, Britain's domestic security service, said in his annual speech that MI5 has caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI, that his greatest concern is bioweapons, a risk "not yet manifest", and that MI5 launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre this year {C12-03}. Fact: The Record reports that AIR, an AI security start-up, found that Vercel's sandbox for running AI-agent code can be tricked into leaking data, with no patch yet and no evidence of exploitation, according to Niv Hoffman, AIR's co-founder and chief technology officer {C12-05}. Fact: Reuters reports that more than two dozen US lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration to pause an AI tool that advises on flights around Washington, having seen no safety evaluation, and want an answer by 19 October; Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, calls it essentially "dumb AI" {C12-09}. Fact: Japan Today reports that Japan is asking Anthropic for help with its cybersecurity, after the hacks on more than 20 companies that our 11 October edition carried; headline only {C12-07}. Fact: The Information reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that OpenAI is in early talks, which could still fall apart, to buy Trail of Bits, which finds and fixes flaws in open-source software {C06-06}, and Constellation Research reports that Anthropic will license technology from Opaque, which keeps data protected while a model processes it, and take on part of its team {C06-08}. Inference: the Booz Allen test of our 12 October edition showed an agent reaching a factory's machinery with a person approving each step; today the warning moves from the factory to the kitchen, and the scientists' letter asks for the brake that Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, designed in our 11 October edition to be made international. The incidents in the entries are smaller and real: a sandbox that leaks and an air-traffic tool whose safety file nobody has seen. The two deals say where the labs think the money is, OpenAI buying the people who fix open-source flaws and Anthropic the people who keep data sealed while the model works; the labs are becoming security companies, which is also what Japan is asking one of them to be.

Fact: Reuters reports that Anthropic asked the US Court of Appeals in Washington on Tuesday to reconsider its 2-1 September ruling, carried in our 7 October edition, that let the Pentagon label it a supply-chain risk after it refused uses of its AI in autonomous weapons and mass surveillance; the court has not said whether it will {C13-01}. Fact: The Associated Press reports that an OpenAI engineer was arrested on 9 October and charged with planting a recording device, found on 30 September in an executive conference room; OpenAI says it traced the device with its own models and has no sign that model weights, code or customer data were taken, and the complaint does not say what the recordings were for {C13-02}. Fact: Reuters reports, citing two people, that Anthropic and OpenAI sought significant control over what outside safety evaluators may publish, which both companies dispute in part, and that OpenAI redacted non-public information from an outside report on the Hugging Face hack {C04-03}. Fact: The Decoder reports that Anthropic says its new defences cut the reasoning data extracted from Claude by 90 to 99 percent, names the Chinese companies Zhipu and Moonshot as participants with no reply from either, and admits that legitimate users are caught too {C01-04}. Inference: the evaluators' story and the London testimony are one story told from two sides: the labs ask in public for binding rules and, by Reuters' account, in private for control over what the testers may say; in our 12 October edition OpenAI said it was close to signing contracts with the testing groups, and the publishing clauses of those contracts are now the question. The Pentagon case decides whether a lab may refuse a use; the bug in the conference room is the reminder that the thing most worth stealing was in the room, not in the model.

sections.title: 4. Infrastructure
paragraphs: Fact: Reuters reports that ASML, the Dutch maker of the machines that print chips, said on 14 October that it cannot fully meet AI-driven demand in 2027 and 2028 and is looking at ways to expand, forecast fourth-quarter sales of 14.2 to 15.2 billion euros, and that Christophe Fouquet, its chief executive, said customers are discussing orders for 2029 and sometimes 2030 {C08-01}. Fact: Reuters reports that IDC, a research firm, estimates Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators to China in the first half of 2026, down 44 percent, for a 34 percent share against Huawei's 28, and that Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, says US export curbs handed China's $50 billion market to Huawei {C07-04}. Fact: Tom's Hardware, relaying the Financial Times, reports that Chinese companies bought more than a million export-compliant Nvidia gaming and workstation chips to cover a shortfall of nearly 1.5 million AI chips, with Chinese factories expected to make about 3.5 million against demand above 5 million; the figures are unnamed insiders' {C08-04}. Fact: Counterpoint Research says China's YMTC rose to third place among NAND flash makers by shipments in the second quarter and is heading for a Shanghai listing, with MS Hwang, Counterpoint's research director, asking whether it can win customers outside China {C08-05}. Fact: Computerworld reports that Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation AI chip, which Scott Guthrie, its executive vice president for cloud and AI, expects to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems; Microsoft plans to deploy it after the turn of the year and make the Maia family its primary AI system from 2027, so the 40 percent is an expectation {C08-02}. Fact: CTech reports that Applied Materials opened a research centre in California where TSMC, Intel, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix will work beside its engineers, with its spending there expected to grow to about $5 billion over time {C08-03}. Fact: TrendForce reports that Hoshik Kim, a senior vice president at SK hynix, said that pooling memory across a server rack cut the wait for an AI answer by three to five times in the company's own tests, and that a flash memory with about 14 times the capacity of high-bandwidth memory is due as samples in early 2028 {C08-07}. Fact: TrendForce reports that Elon Musk, chief executive of Tesla, wrote on Wednesday that Micron "has been reasonable regarding future memory prices, while others have been extortionate", naming no one, and Reuters reports that Micron's customer commitments reached $32 billion by September, up from $22 billion in June {C08-06}. Fact: CTech reports that Nvidia made the full code of Run:ai, software that splits graphics chips between jobs, open source while still selling supported versions {C03-02}. Inference: the shortage story of the past week got its longest horizon today: the company that makes the machines that make the chips says it cannot fully meet demand in 2027 and 2028, and the biggest buyers' answers are all ways around it, Microsoft's own chip, SK hynix's pooled memory, Nvidia's open-sourced scheduler, Chinese companies buying gaming cards. The memory makers now have a buyer calling them extortionate, and Micron's $32 billion of commitments says the sellers are locking in the price while it lasts. Set beside the Korean selling in section 5, the entries describe a market in which supply is sold out to 2028 and chipmakers' shares fell for a fifth day in Seoul while the main US chip index headed for a sixth straight fall, which is consistent only if what is being sold is the price, not the volume.

Fact: Nikkei Asia reports, citing several sources, that NTT Data is in late-stage talks to build a 500 megawatt data centre in Osaka for Anthropic at about 1 trillion yen before servers and chips, with partial operation possible by 2028 and on-site generation under study because the grid cannot easily supply that much power; neither company has commented {C09-05}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that Jeff Bleich, Anthropic's international special envoy, told a Sydney summit that state premiers have pitched sites and that Anthropic prefers regional, renewable-powered ones, with no site, sum or timetable {C09-08}. Fact: The Business Times reports that seven banks arranged a further $3.7 billion for DayOne's data-centre campus in Johor, Malaysia, doubling its financing there, with DayOne's US listing filed on 6 October {C09-12}. Fact: Reuters reports, citing two people with direct knowledge, that AirTrunk, the data-centre operator owned by Blackstone, postponed a Singapore listing that could raise about $1.5 billion because of the AI share sell-off, after Firmus scrapped its own; no new date is set {C06-09}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that Oracle renewed its plea to federal regulators for a gas pipeline to power its New Mexico campus, which has slipped to February 2027, while Raul Torrez, the state's attorney general, demands a fuller environmental review {C09-14}. Fact: Politico's Surge newsletter says a slowdown in data-centre development has arrived; headline only {C09-11}. Inference: the map of our 12 October edition, Sydney out of spare power, Thailand suspending 49 projects, banks near their limits, has today's additions: Asia still lends, Johor's financing doubled, and still builds, Osaka with the power to be made on site because the grid cannot give 500 megawatts, while the listed exits close, AirTrunk after Firmus. Oracle's pipeline is the US version of Osaka, the computer ready before the power. Scenario: if Politico's slowdown is real, it shows first in these financings, a loan not doubled, a listing not revived.

sections.title: 5. Markets
paragraphs: Fact: Reuters reports in an analysis that Tuesday brought the heaviest selling of AI supplier shares since late July, with South Korea's main index down more than 6 percent on a fifth day of chipmaker falls, Kioxia, the Japanese memory maker, down 13 percent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index heading for a sixth straight fall, on worries that rising interest rates could derail a spending boom bigger than the US railroad boom; Marc Velan, head of investments at Lucerne Asset Management in Singapore, says the session says more about positioning and the cost of capital than about demand, though "Korea could be an early warning of a broader shakeout" {C07-01}. Fact: CGTN reports that the International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday in Bangkok, names the possible end of the AI investment boom, a prolonged Middle East war and rising debt as the main risks, forecasts world growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz reopens by March 2027 and AI investment holds, and says a steep fall in AI investment could cut US output by 1.8 percent and world output by 1.1 percent by 2028; Petya Koeva-Brooks, deputy director of the Fund's research department, says the world economy's resilience "may be reaching its limits" and the boom lifts few countries {C07-02}. Fact: Semafor reports that Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said price rises tied to the AI boom are "jumping out of its lane" into unrelated parts of the economy, which he fears is "straight, old-fashioned overheating demand", and that if inflation persists "it's clear what the Fed has to do"; he does not vote on rates until 2027, and September's inflation figures are due this week {C05-05}. Fact: The WealthAdvisor reports that Bank of America's October survey of 161 fund managers found a net 37 percent holding more technology shares than their benchmark, the most since 2020, 45 percent expecting an AI bubble in 2027 against 42 who do not, semiconductors the most crowded trade and a disorderly rise in bond yields the biggest threat {C07-07}. Inference: forecast 3 of our 12 October edition, that the Fund would name AI among the main risks, came true on Tuesday with a number attached, 1.8 percent of US output. The week's sequence is: the lenders repriced on Monday, in our 12 October edition; the Fund quantified on Tuesday; the market sold on Tuesday, a fifth day in Seoul, with the main US chip index heading for a sixth; and a Fed president tied the boom to inflation. The survey explains the selling better than demand does: the managers are more overweight technology than at any time since 2020 and almost half expect a bubble, which is a crowd standing near the exit. Unknown: how much of the Korean fall is foreign money leaving, which Bloomberg put at 131 billion dollars this year in our 11 October edition.

Fact: Bloomberg reports that Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive of Meta, said on the Cheeky Pint podcast that Meta committed hundreds of billions of dollars to AI infrastructure before knowing whether it would pay off, recalling that he asked Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, "You sure this is going to work?", and the Hindustan Times adds that Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, warned of the cost of failure and that Meta reports on 21 October; it is his recollection of past doubt, not a sign the spending has failed {C05-03}. Fact: Barron's reports that Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla, answered "No crying in the casino" to Hock Tan, chief executive of Broadcom, the US chip maker, who said in Singapore on Monday, by Bloomberg's account, that many AI investors "have no clue" what they are putting money into; it is a quip with no figures, continuing the item our 12 October edition carried {C05-04}. Fact: CNBC reports, citing two people, that Anthropic shows institutional investors its third-quarter figures for the first time at a meeting on Wednesday 14 October, ahead of a listing that a relay citing Reuters puts in November; Anthropic declined to comment and nothing is confirmed {C06-01}. Fact: The Standard of Hong Kong reports, citing unnamed mainland media, that DeepSeek's second funding round has doubled to 100 billion yuan at an unchanged valuation of about 500 billion yuan, with CATL and Geely among the investors and a Shanghai listing expected to follow; the round is not closed {C06-02}. Fact: Shuli Ren, a Bloomberg Opinion columnist, argues that public investors now ask when AI cloud companies break even, citing Firmus's failed share sale and AirTrunk's delay, and that CoreWeave is expected to make $7.6 billion of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation this year against capital spending of up to $39 billion; it is one columnist's reading of two listings {C07-06}. Fact: The Information reports that Applied Intuition, a maker of self-driving software, has investment offers at $30 billion or more, double its June valuation, with no word that it has accepted one {C06-07}; Business Insider reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that Decagon, which builds customer-support agents, hired a bank to weigh a sale after early talks with ServiceNow, which says they are no longer ongoing {C06-11}; TechCrunch reports that Character.AI filed for bankruptcy with assets and liabilities of $50 million to $100 million and a sale expected to close in late November or early December {C06-03}. Inference: the week's confession is Zuckerberg's: the bet was placed before the answer, and the answer comes on 21 October. Private money is still paying up, DeepSeek at 500 billion yuan, Applied Intuition at double, Astribot's fourth round in six months, while public money closes its window, AirTrunk after Firmus, and a consumer chat app goes bankrupt; the gap between those two prices is where Anthropic's investor meeting, reported by CNBC from two people, lands today, the first time its figures would be shown to the people who would buy the listing. Musk's line is the market's mood in five words, and Tan's is the warning it answers. Markets share of this analysis: section 5 is about 11 percent of the words; counting the market material in the forecasts and the watch list as well, about 25 percent.

sections.title: Forecasts
paragraphs: 1. The 2027 spending plans of Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon at their results this season, in three scenarios that exclude each other and together cover every outcome, so they add up to 100 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks, with Meta on 21 October (Meta's own notice of 12 October, found today), Alphabet on 28 October (Alphabet's own investor site, announced 6 October, found today), Microsoft on 28 October (its investor page, as checked for our 11 October edition) and Amazon not confirmed. Confidence: low. (a) None of the four trims or defers its 2027 plan: probability 55 percent, down from 60 on 12 October. Signal: ASML sold out through 2028 {C08-01}, Meta's Kentucky deal {C09-13}, Microsoft's own chip for 2027 {C08-02}, DayOne's doubled financing {C09-12}. (b) Exactly one trims or defers: 35 percent, up from 30. Signal: the reported cost cuts inside Microsoft's Azure group, which Microsoft disputes {C06-05}; Zuckerberg describing the bet as made without proof {C05-03}; Oregon's pause in Amazon's state {C09-01}. (c) Two or more trim or defer: 10 percent. Signal: the Fund's 1.8 percent {C07-02}, the fifth day of Korean selling {C07-01}, Goolsbee's overheating {C05-05} and the survey's crowded trade {C07-07}. The move from (a) to (b) is because a report of cost cuts inside the cloud that spends most, even a disputed one, is the first sign from inside a spender. Confirms or weakens each: the guidance itself. Affects: the towns and suppliers waiting on the build first, then savers in index funds, then the memory makers whose next quarter Korea is pricing.

2. An AI-linked borrower prices a bond or loan deal of 10 billion dollars or more before the Federal Reserve's decision on 28 October. Probability 45 percent, down from 55 on 12 October. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: low. Signal: DayOne's 3.7 billion dollars is under the bar {C09-12}; AirTrunk's postponement {C06-09} and Firmus's failed sale {C07-06} say the public window is shut; against that, Osaka's 1 trillion yen will need financing {C09-05}. Confirms: a priced deal reported by the borrower or a wire. Weakens: another postponement, or Tencent's 5 billion dollar sale of our 12 October edition pricing smaller than planned. Affects: savers in bond funds first, then borrowers outside AI that wait their turn, then the builders.

3. TSMC, at its results conference on 15 October, guides fourth-quarter revenue above the 44.6 to 45.8 billion dollars it guided for the third quarter (TSMC's own investor site, found today) and does not cut its 2026 capital spending plan. Probability 75 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: ASML's two sold-out years {C08-01}, China's shortfall of 1.5 million chips and its buying of gaming cards {C08-04}, and Argon's rollout at scale {C01-01}; against it, the investor Reuters quotes reads the selling as the cost of capital, not demand {C07-01}. Confirms: the guidance. Weakens: a flat outlook or a spending cut, which would be the first crack in supply-side demand and would move scenario 1(a) down again. Affects: savers in chip-heavy funds first, then Taiwan's and Korea's economies, then the AI buyers who hold the contracts.

4. A smartphone, PC or chip maker confirms in its own words, a price list, a results call or a filing, a price rise or a shipment cut tied to memory supply by mid-November; this continues forecast 5 of our 12 October edition. Probability 70 percent, up from 60. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: medium. Signal: Counterpoint's 20 percent fall in shipments with Xiaomi down more than 30 percent {C08-08}, Musk's "extortionate" {C08-06}, Micron's 32 billion dollars of commitments {C08-06} and a gaming card at 7,199 dollars {C08-04}. Confirms: a company statement; Samsung and SK hynix report in late October, on dates not yet confirmed by them. Weakens: the production cuts Counterpoint expects not appearing in company results. Affects: phone buyers first, then the cheaper brands, then the memory makers and the AI buyers holding contracts.

5. The UK publishes a bill text or a formal consultation on compulsory AI safety or incident reporting within 3 months. Probability 60 percent, up from 50 on 12 October. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: low. Signal: Anthropic and OpenAI asking MPs for binding rules starting with incident reporting {C13-03}; the institute keeping its early access {C12-08}; Nvidia's 250 million dollars announced with the minister {C12-04}; MI5's new centre {C12-03}; against it, Google DeepMind and Meta {C13-03} and a US President who calls the danger a hoax {C05-01}. Confirms: a published text. Weakens: a consultation with no duty in it, or a US-UK understanding that defers to voluntary pledges. Affects: the people whose systems agents reach first, then the labs, then insurers.

6. Chinese models hold first place on OpenRouter's weekly usage ranking in each of the next 4 weeks. Probability 70 percent, down from 80 on 12 October. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: Argon at a fifth of its rivals' prices {C01-01} is the first US price cut, the weakening signal we named on 12 October; DeepSeek's 100 billion yuan {C06-02} and Nature's researcher count {C04-05} support the lead; Anthropic's bans of accounts routing through Claude {C01-04} do not touch the count. Confirms: the weekly counts. Weakens: Argon or another US model taking first place in any week. Affects: developers choosing on price first, then the US labs' pricing, then the chip makers whose customers run these models.

7. A buyer announces a bid that keeps Character.ai running, filed with the court by the sale deadline. Probability 60 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: low. Signal: Disney's 20 million dollar licence, on the company's account, and more than 20 million monthly users {C14-15}; against it, the lawsuits and TechCrunch's reading that costs rise with use {C06-03}. Confirms: a bid on the court docket. Weakens: a wind-down notice. Affects: the users and the families suing first, then the staff, then Disney.

8. Churchill Capital Corp XI's shareholders approve the Agility Robotics merger on 2 November and it closes in November as planned. Probability 70 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: low. Signal: the registration declared effective and a 200 million dollar private sale led by Foxconn {C11-03}; Korea's state-backed humanoid pilot {C11-10}; against it, the sell-off that stopped AirTrunk {C06-09} and redemptions that could cut the 424 million dollars in the trust. Confirms: the vote and a Nasdaq debut. Weakens: a postponed vote or heavy redemptions. Affects: Agility's workers and customers first, then its investors, then the humanoid makers raising money on its price.
9. Amazon announces an agreement to buy Decart, the chip-software start-up of our 12 October edition, within 4 weeks of that date: unchanged at 55 percent, with no new signal in today's entries.

sections.title: A. Highest conviction developments to watch
paragraphs: The dates below come from the day's entries, from the companies and institutions themselves, or from published calendars, and each one says where it comes from and whether we could confirm it today. Where a date is not confirmed, it says so.

1. Wednesday 14 October: US consumer prices for September, 8:30 a.m. Eastern, on third-party calendars that attribute the date to the Bureau of Labor Statistics; the Bureau's own schedule page, opened today, lists releases only from 10 November on, so we could not confirm it there, and Semafor says the figures are due this week {C05-05}. Why: Goolsbee's overheating is the link between the build and interest rates, and Reuters' account of Tuesday's selling names rates as the worry {C07-01}. Also 14 October: Anthropic's first showing of its quarterly figures to institutional investors (CNBC, citing two people) {C06-01}; whatever is learned of its growth and losses sets the price of a listing that is reported for November, not confirmed. Also this week, no date given: the President's planned meeting with AI executives (ABC News, from the Speaker of the House, with no White House confirmation) {C05-01}.

2. Thursday 15 October, 2 p.m. Taiwan time: TSMC's third-quarter earnings conference (TSMC's own investor page, found today through a search of it; the company's quiet period ran to 14 October). Why: forecast 3; after ASML {C08-01} it is the second supplier to say how far demand runs, and a raised outlook would say supply is still the limit. Also 15 October: G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meet with the Financial Stability Board's AI letter and practices before them (the FSB's own release, carried in our 12 October edition; not rechecked today), two days after the Fund's numbers {C07-02}.

3. Friday 16 October: a SpaceX representative answers the New York City Council on AI safety (New York Post, citing the Council Speaker) {C13-04}, and the Energy Department's emergency order for the PJM grid expires (The National) {C09-03}. Why: the first test of a city's power to make a lab answer; and whether any data centre was actually told to run on its own generators, which the order's wording leaves open.

4. Monday 19 October: the lawmakers' deadline for the Federal Aviation Administration to answer on its AI flight tool (Reuters) {C12-09}; China's third-quarter growth data, 10 a.m. Beijing time on a third-party calendar, not confirmed from the National Bureau of Statistics; the Fund says the boom lifts few countries {C07-02}, and the chip counts {C07-04} {C08-04} make China's quarter the first measured check; and the FDA's comment deadline on AI tools that act as doctors (KFF Health News, carried in our 9 October edition; not rechecked today). Tuesday 20 October: the Memphis City Council's rescheduled vote on a 12-month pause on data centres (Fox News, carried in our 8 October edition; not rechecked today), after Oregon {C09-01} and Milwaukee {C09-04}.

5. Wednesday 21 October, after the US close: Meta's third-quarter results, with the call at 1:30 p.m. Pacific (Meta's own notice of 12 October, found today; the Hindustan Times gives the same date {C05-03}). Why: the first of the four spenders of forecast 1, and the one whose chief executive said the bet was made before the proof; the 2027 capital spending line is the number. Also 21 October: Tesla's results (Tesla's own notice, as checked for our 11 October edition; not rechecked today), the first time Musk answers analysts after "No crying in the casino" {C05-04} and the school-zone petition {C11-01}.

6. 27 October, not confirmed by the company: SK hynix's third-quarter results, on third-party calendars, one of which says 28 October. 29 October, not confirmed: Samsung's full third-quarter results, as in our 12 October edition. Why: five days of selling of Korean chipmaker shares {C07-01} is a bet on their next quarter; their price guidance tests forecast 4, Musk's "extortionate" {C08-06} and SK hynix's own memory plans {C08-07}.

7. 27 to 28 October: the Federal Reserve meets, with the decision at 2 p.m. Eastern on 28 October (the Federal Reserve's own calendar, as opened for our 12 October edition). 28 October: Alphabet's results, with the call at 1:30 p.m. Pacific (Alphabet's own investor site, announced 6 October, found today), and Microsoft's results (its investor page, as checked for our 11 October edition). Amazon: no date from the company was found; third-party calendars say 29 October, which is not a confirmation. Why: the Fed sets the price of the debt in section 5, and Goolsbee has said what persistent inflation would make it do {C05-05}; the three results decide forecast 1.

8. 2 November: Churchill Capital Corp XI's shareholders vote on the Agility merger (Agility's own release) {C11-03}. 3 November: the US midterm elections, a date fixed by law, with data centres an issue in the Oregon {C09-01} and Nevada {C09-10} governors' races and on the local ballots WIRED counted in our 12 October edition. Mid-November, not confirmed: Nvidia's results, which third-party calendars put on 18 November, with no notice from Nvidia found today. End of November: Argon's introductory price doubles {C01-01}; Character.ai's sale is expected to close in late November or early December {C06-03}; Agility expects its Nasdaq debut in November {C11-03}; Apple's HomeView ships next month {C02-02}; and Anthropic's listing is reported for November by a relay citing Reuters, not confirmed {C06-01}.

Further out, from the entries: Oregon's permit pause to July 2027 {C09-01}; Oracle's pipeline, slipped to February 2027 {C09-14}; Microsoft's Maia 300, deployed after the turn of the year and primary from 2027 {C08-02}; Osaka's partial operation possibly by 2028, from unnamed sources, not confirmed {C09-05}; SK hynix's flash samples in early 2028 {C08-07}; ASML's two sold-out years {C08-01}; AirTrunk's aim to list by early 2027, from one unnamed source, not confirmed {C06-09}; and the data from Korea's 20 humanoids {C11-10}. Without a date, but decisive: the appeals court's answer to Anthropic {C13-01}; Vercel's patch {C12-05}; the Trail of Bits and Decagon talks {C06-06} {C06-11}; the Caine Prize's finding {C14-03}; the evaluators' contracts {C04-03}; and whether Politico's slowdown comes with numbers {C09-11}.

sections.title: B. Low probability, high impact scenarios
paragraphs: 1. A forced-selling chain in AI shares that reaches credit markets and jobs, the scenario UNCTAD described in our 10 October edition; today's signals are a 6 percent day in Seoul {C07-01}, the Fund's 1.8 percent {C07-02} and semiconductors as the most crowded trade {C07-07}. Probability: under 10 percent in 3 months. 2. A confirmed AI worm spreading through home devices within the months Anthropic's red team names {C12-01}. Probability: under 5 percent in 3 months. 3. The full appeals court grants Anthropic's rehearing and reverses the Pentagon's label {C13-01}. Probability: about 10 percent in 3 months. 4. The White House moves from posts to a written order that blocks federal or state AI safety rules {C05-01}. Probability: about 10 percent in 3 months. 5. A large AI-linked listing, Anthropic's, DeepSeek's, DayOne's or Agility's, is pulled after launch, the Firmus outcome at many times the size {C06-01} {C06-02} {C09-12} {C11-03}. Probability: about 15 percent in 3 months. 6. A second US state follows Oregon with a statewide pause on data-centre permits before the midterms {C09-01}. Probability: about 15 percent in 4 weeks. 7. TSMC cuts its 2026 spending plan on Thursday {C08-01}. Probability: under 10 percent.

sections.title: C. Signals that would change this view
paragraphs: Toward more risk: a flat TSMC outlook on Thursday; a hot September inflation print; a sixth and seventh day of Korean selling with foreign money still leaving {C07-01}; Meta trimming its 2027 plan on 21 October {C05-03}; Samsung or SK hynix guiding to softer memory prices {C08-06}; Microsoft confirming the Azure cuts {C06-05}; Politico's slowdown arriving with numbers {C09-11}; a Fed that holds rates with Goolsbee's language {C05-05}. Toward less risk: TSMC raising its outlook and spending; Meta's 2027 plan up with the cash to pay for it; a 10 billion dollar deal pricing tight; foreign money returning to Korea; AirTrunk relaunching its listing {C06-09}; a soft inflation print. Toward a different story: a UK bill text, which moves forecast 5 to confirmed {C13-03}; the appeals court granting a rehearing {C13-01}; the President's meeting producing a written pledge {C05-01}; Argon taking OpenRouter's first place {C01-01}; a court bid for Character.ai {C14-15}; the FAA producing its safety file {C12-09}; Korea's robots working unfenced for a month without incident {C11-10}; and a worm found outside a lab {C12-01}, which would make Anthropic's months a date.

sections.title: D. Key unknowns and data gaps
paragraphs: Unknown: the figures Anthropic is reported to show investors today {C06-01}; how much of the Korean fall is foreign selling {C07-01}; whether the Azure cost cuts are real, which Microsoft denies {C06-05}; the insiders behind the Financial Times' count of China's chips {C08-04}; what OpenAI's loop transformers do to oversight {C01-02}; who controlled the robot in Cologne {C11-13}; whether any data centre was switched to back-up power under the emergency order {C09-03}; what the evaluators' contracts will let the testers publish {C04-03}; what progress on the Riemann hypothesis Science describes {C04-01}; the terms of the Opaque, ConductorOne and Decart deals {C06-08} {C02-04}; and the date of Trump's meeting with the executives {C05-01}. Missing data: known to us from headlines only are Science on Riemann {C04-01}, POLITICO Europe on Europe's leaders {C13-06}, Politico on the slowdown {C09-11}, Bloomberg's 5 trillion dollar market {C11-06}, the Journal on Walmart {C11-08}, Phoronix on the Linux kernel {C03-03} and Japan Today on Anthropic {C12-07}; the Journal on utilities was read through a summary {C09-07}, and The Information's reports on OpenAI's design, Azure, Trail of Bits and Applied Intuition only to their paywalls or through relays {C01-02} {C06-05} {C06-06} {C06-07}. Missing data: Reuters on the chip selling, Nvidia's China share, Harris, the appeals court, the evaluators, DeepMind's Europe scheme, AirTrunk, Zealand and the aviation tool; Reuters on ASML, Apple's HomeView and the SPUR coalition {C08-01} {C02-02} {C13-05}; Bloomberg on Zuckerberg, Alibaba, Australia, Oracle, the Deloitte survey and Winverse; CNBC on Anthropic; Barron's on Musk; the Associated Press on Kroger, Nevada and the OpenAI engineer; Nikkei Asia on Osaka; and the Financial Times on China's chips were all read through relays, wire copies or excerpts, and the originals were not opened {C07-01} {C07-04} {C05-07} {C13-01} {C04-03} {C04-04} {C06-09} {C06-10} {C12-09} {C05-03} {C11-11} {C09-08} {C09-14} {C14-02} {C11-12} {C06-01} {C05-04} {C14-01} {C09-10} {C13-02} {C09-05} {C08-04}; the IMF's outlook was read in CGTN's report, not the Fund's document {C07-02}. Missing data: the dates of the September US inflation release, the SK hynix, Samsung, Amazon and Nvidia results, China's growth data and Anthropic's listing could not be confirmed from their own sources today; the Microsoft, Tesla, Federal Reserve, G20, FDA and Memphis dates rest on earlier checks; the TSMC, Meta and Alphabet dates were confirmed from the companies' own pages today.
This is analysis of the news, not financial advice or an investment recommendation.
